theme: Heartbreak, bonds & raising kids · 사랑의 뇌과학과 사교육 경쟁

tracks.title: Why does heartbreak hurt so much?
tracks.note: 실연이 왜 '진짜로' 아픈지 뇌과학으로 설명해요. 사회적 관계(social bonds)가 수명과 면역에 주는 영향도 나와서 임상 쪽 관심사와도 잘 맞아요. 1회차는 대략적인 내용만, 2회차는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Hi Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Hi Neil.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Now, I want you to think back to the last time you had your heart broken.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: How did it feel?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: It was a couple of years ago.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And I just remember a really intense, sad emotion.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: But it also sometimes feels like a physical pain in your stomach, doesn't it?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: It does.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: It's like real pain, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: And today, in 6 Minute English, we're talking about heartbreak.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Now, heartbreak is the feeling of sadness we get when we lose someone we love.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: And that pain you feel, it's not just imaginary.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: In this podcast, we'll be understanding how our brains change when we fall in love and asking the question, why does heartbreak hurt so much?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And as usual, we'll be learning some useful new vocabulary.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: You can find the full list and the definitions at bbclearningenglish.com.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Georgie, we're going to start with a quiz question.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Are you ready?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: I am very ready.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: So, in the 1950s, psychologists noticed a link between children's early bonds with their parents and their romantic relationships as adults, but what is this theory called?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Is it: a) contraction theory, b) attachment theory, or c) superstition theory?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: I think it's b) attachment theory.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, we will find out at the end of the programme.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: What's going on in our brains when we fall in love?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, scientists have scanned people's brains while they're looking at a photo of their romantic partner.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: And they found that looking at someone you're in love with activates a part of the brain that also reminds us to eat and drink.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And do scientists know why being in love impacts our brain in this way?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: So, it's all about survival.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Our brains have evolved to be this way.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Dr Lucy Brown explains more to the BBC World Service.

transcript.speaker: Dr Lucy Brown
transcript.text: This is a survival system.

transcript.speaker: Dr Lucy Brown
transcript.text: Nature gave us these systems to be addicted to each other – for reproduction, for protection.

transcript.speaker: Dr Lucy Brown
transcript.text: You're oriented completely toward the other person.

transcript.speaker: Dr Lucy Brown
transcript.text: It's like hunger or thirst.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Lucy says our brains make us addicted to our romantic partners.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: If you're addicted to something, you want more of it.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: You can literally be addicted to things like drugs or alcohol, but we also use it metaphorically to talk about things we love.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: She says that romantic partners are oriented to each other, which in British English we say orientated, and it means they are pointed towards each other.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: They think of each other before other people.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Neil, is there anything else scientists have discovered from scanning the brains of people in love?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, being in love doesn't just change the way we think.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: It changes our whole identity.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: A 2013 study showed us more about this.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: People were shown statements about themselves – for example, Neil is kind – and the part of the brain we use to think about ourselves lit up.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: When showing the same statements about their partner, the same part of the brain was active – not the part of the brain we generally use to think about others.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, Neil, are all of these brain changes that come with being in love actually good for us?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, studies suggest that good social connections help manage stress and support our immune system.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Professor Zoe Donaldson explained more to the BBC World Service.

transcript.speaker: Professor Zoe Donaldson
transcript.text: Having really strong social bonds increases your likelihood that you'll survive from just about anything, whether that be cancer, depression, etc.

transcript.speaker: Professor Zoe Donaldson
transcript.text: And it overall is the number one predictor of longevity.

transcript.speaker: Professor Zoe Donaldson
transcript.text: So, if you are lonely and you don't have bonds, then your mortality risk goes up in a way that's equivalent to being obese or smoking.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, having strong social bonds or close relationships with other people makes you more likely to survive disease, according to Zoe.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Yes, it's an important factor in our longevity, which means how long we live.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: In fact, Zoe says, being lonely and not having good social bonds increases your mortality risk, your risk of dying, by as much as being obese or smoking.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, what happens when these bonds are broken, when we experience heartbreak?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, scientists have been looking at this by asking people to look at photos of their exes, their former partners, and scanning their brains.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: They found that heartbreak activates parts of the brain we use when we're in danger or in pain.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Professor Zoe Donaldson explains more.

transcript.speaker: Professor Zoe Donaldson
transcript.text: It's literal pain in your brain.

transcript.speaker: Professor Zoe Donaldson
transcript.text: So, if you look at the parts of the brain that light up, they overlap with the same brain regions that are activated when you feel visceral pain – when you feel actual, you know... like you get a burn, or you break a... you break a bone.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: So, now it's time for the answer to the quiz question I asked you.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: It was about a theory developed by psychologists in the 1950s, which says that children's early relationships with their parents impact their relationships as adults.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: What's the name of the theory?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: I was quite confident about this, wasn't I, Neil?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: I said attachment theory.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, you had a reason to be confident because you are correct.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Yay!

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Let's recap the vocabulary we learnt in this programme, starting with heartbreak, which is the feeling you experience after you lose someone you love.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: If you're addicted to someone or something, you want more of it all the time.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Oriented or orientated towards is used metaphorically to mean that someone or something is your main focus.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Social bonds are the close relationships we have with family, friends and romantic partners.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Longevity means how long you'll live.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: And an ex is a past romantic partner that you are no longer in a relationship with.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Once again, our six minutes are up, but you can test what you've learned with the worksheet on our website.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Go to bbclearningenglish.com.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Thanks for joining us and goodbye.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Goodbye.

listening.task: 6 Minute English를 한 번은 대략적인 내용만 듣고, 두 번째는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요. 그다음 퀴즈에 답해 보세요. 'social bonds'와 'longevity'가 나오는 부분을 잘 들어 보세요.

quiz.q: In the 1950s, psychologists linked children's early bonds with their parents to their adult romantic relationships. What is this theory called? a) contraction theory, b) attachment theory, c) superstition theory
quiz.answer: b) attachment theory (애착 이론). 보너스: 외로움(사회적 관계 부족)은 비만이나 흡연과 비슷한 수준으로 사망 위험(mortality risk)을 높인대요.

sentences.text: Now, heartbreak is the feeling of sadness we get when we lose someone we love.
sentences.ko: 이제 heartbreak(실연의 아픔)는 사랑하는 사람을 잃었을 때 느끼는 슬픔이에요.

sentences.text: Our brains have evolved to be this way.
sentences.ko: 우리 뇌는 이런 방식으로 진화해 왔어요.

sentences.text: Well, studies suggest that good social connections help manage stress and support our immune system.
sentences.ko: 연구에 따르면 좋은 사회적 관계는 스트레스를 다스리고 면역 체계를 돕는대요.

sentences.text: Yes, it's an important factor in our longevity, which means how long we live.
sentences.ko: 네, 그건 우리의 수명(longevity), 즉 얼마나 오래 사는지에 중요한 요인이에요.

sentences.text: Well, you had a reason to be confident because you are correct.

reading.title: Intensive parenting is no longer the preserve of the rich
reading.summaryKo: 대학·좋은 일자리 경쟁이 치열해지면서 소득과 상관없이 모든 계층의 부모가 사교육·스포츠에 더 일찍, 더 많이 돈을 써요. 한국은 학령기 아동 4명 중 3명이 사교육을 받고(최저소득층도 57%), 자녀 1인당 평생 교육투자의 42%(약 15만 2천 달러)를 가계가 부담해요. 하지만 부자들도 손을 놓지 않아 계층 이동은 오히려 정체됐다는 내용이에요. (공개 전재본 기준 발췌)
excerpt: RICH PARENTS are different. They have money. They also used to be different in spending pots of it on their offspring’s edification. Yet as competition for university places and well-paying jobs heats up, parents across income levels are bankrolling their children’s futures earlier and more aggressively.

As with young bodies, so with young minds. Private tutoring has long been an obsession in richer parts of Asia. Three in four school-age South Koreans took paid lessons in 2025, according to national surveys, including 57% in the lowest income quintile. So did four in five five-year-olds.
reading.tip: 'bankroll'(돈을 대다), 'heat up'(과열되다)처럼 돈·경쟁 관련 동사가 많아요. 'Three in four ..., including 57% in the lowest income quintile'은 통계를 말할 때 그대로 쓸 수 있는 구조예요. 목동 학부모로서 공감하며 읽어 보세요.

vocab.example: Strong social bonds help us manage stress.
Social bonds are the number one predictor of longevity.
Loneliness raises your mortality risk as much as smoking.
Parents are bankrolling their children's futures earlier.
Private tutoring has long been an obsession in Asia.
The poor are spending more, but the rich are not letting up.

writing.prompt: Is spending more on private tutoring worth it for young children? Write 3–5 sentences in English, using your own experience as a parent in Mokdong.
writing.question: What do you want your children to learn outside school, and why?
writing.hint: 이런 표현을 써 보세요: In Korea, most parents ... / I think ... is worth it because ... / However, the rich are not letting up, so ... / For my kids, I care more about ...

speaking.prompt: In one minute, explain to a friend why heartbreak can feel like real physical pain, and why strong social bonds are good for your health.
phrases: It activates the same parts of the brain as ...
Strong social bonds are linked with ...
Being lonely raises your mortality risk.
speaking.alt: 쉬운 버전: How many after-school classes do your kids take? Do you think it's too many?

evening.note: 화요일이에요. 어제 이어서 10페이지. 오늘은 서우 생일이니 🎂 가족과 시간 보내고, 5페이지만 읽어도 충분해요. Minimum day도 OK.
